It's inexact though. Because not all money that changes hands is actually taxed as personal income, or even corporate income for that matter. I'm no fan of taxation, and the spirit of the post is true, but be prepared to consider that it's actually much more complicated.

The real problem with any taxation, issues of morality aside, is that by taxing something you encourage people to find value in things that aren't taxed as highly. So as far as money changing hands, we have major taxes on a few key things: Personal income, corporate income, and capital gains. What this means is that by taxing these things, people will structure their transactions to avoid paying these taxes, or at least to avoid paying them multiple times over. Capital gains taxes discourage people from cashing in investments in certain situations to avoid this. But there are exceptions if you reinvest those capital gains, but generally only if you reinvest in a similar class of investments. So selling stocks to buy real estate or real estate to buy gold etc. can lead to adverse tax consequences, keeping money in the stock markets where it doesn't really want to be. Income tax can be avoided by diverting it into 401k, or rather, if its paid to you not as cash but as a 401k contribution or health insurance. This tax again puts money into the stock market where it wouldn't otherwise be and creates our mess of a healthcare situation. Corporate income tax spurs bad investment because tax pressure causes companies to offset potential profits with expenditures they might not otherwise make.

The point is not to say that these things are good or bad, but the myriad complicated ways that our tax code operates amount to a tremendous impact on the economy in ways that can't be predicted beforehand.
